title: Keep head and tail correct in a linked FIFO queue
sources: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms, Lecture 2 and Problem Session 1: sequence data structures (Spring 2020)
masterChecklist: Core data structures: arrays/lists, stacks, queues, dequeues, hash tables, linked structures, priority queues, trees, graphs
Problem decomposition, specifications, preconditions/postconditions, invariants, and proofs by reasoning
whyItMatters: A linked queue must preserve arrival order while adding at one end and removing at the other. The hardest bugs happen when its last node leaves and head or tail still points at an old node.
simpleExplanation: A FIFO queue returns the oldest waiting item first. In a singly linked implementation, head points at that item and tail points at the newest. If empty, both are None. To enqueue into an empty queue, set both pointers to the new node; otherwise link tail.next to it and update tail. To dequeue, move head forward; if the removed node was the last one, also set tail to None. Each end operation changes a constant number of references, but scanning for an arbitrary item remains linear. In normal Python applications, collections.deque already supplies efficient end operations and avoids custom pointer-maintenance code.
mentalModel: A line has a front door and a back door. The first arrival leaves from the front; the newest joins at the back. When the final person leaves, both doors point to an empty line.
outcomes: State the empty and nonempty head/tail invariants.
Implement constant-reference-change enqueue and dequeue operations.
Test the one-item boundary and justify using deque in production.

realWorldExample.scenario: A learning app processes submitted practice checks in their arrival order.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: A stale tail after the final dequeue can cause the next enqueue to attach to a node no longer reachable from head.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Write invariant tests for empty, one-item, and repeated enqueue/dequeue transitions; use deque for the actual application queue.

explanation: The first enqueue sets both head and tail.
The second enqueue changes old tail.next and then tail.
Dequeue advances head, preserving oldest-first order.
After removing the final node, tail must become None too.
workedExample.safeExperiment: After both dequeues, enqueue 'third' and confirm it is reachable as the new head and tail.

procedure: Begin with head = tail = None and state the invariant that both are None exactly when empty.
Enqueue by linking a new node after tail, or setting head if the queue was empty; update tail in both cases.
Dequeue by saving head.value, advancing head, and clearing tail if head became None.
Test empty, one-item, multiple-item, and empty-then-refill transitions.
Use deque for application code unless learning or a special linked representation is the reason for custom nodes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving tail pointing to the removed last node.
commonMistakes.why: A later enqueue may attach to an unreachable chain.
commonMistakes.avoid: Set tail to None whenever advancing head makes it None.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to set head on the first enqueue.
commonMistakes.why: The new node exists but cannot be reached for removal.
commonMistakes.avoid: Handle empty and nonempty cases separately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a Python list with repeated pop(0) for a growing FIFO queue.
commonMistakes.avoid: Use collections.deque.popleft in real Python code.

lab.title: Implement and test a linked FIFO queue
lab.safety: All practice data remains fictional and in the local browser worker.
guidedSteps: Create a node for each new value.
If tail is None, make the new node head; otherwise link it after the old tail.
Always make the new node tail.
On removal, save head.value and move head forward; when the new head is None, clear tail.
Run the supplied boundary tests and explain each pointer state.
checks: After final removal, both head and tail are None.
Refilling an emptied queue works and empty removal raises IndexError.
hints: The old tail's next should point to the new node.
After self.head = self.head.next, check if self.head is None.
Save the removed value before changing head.
lab.solutionExplanation: The two pointers identify both ends; each operation changes only a bounded number of links. Resetting tail when the final node leaves preserves the empty-state invariant.
lab.testCode:
q = LinkedQueue()
assert q.head is None and q.tail is None
q.enqueue('A')
q.enqueue('B')
assert q.head.value == 'A' and q.tail.value == 'B'
assert q.dequeue() == 'A'
assert q.dequeue() == 'B'
assert q.head is None and q.tail is None
print('PASS: FIFO and empty invariant')
q.enqueue('C')
assert q.head is q.tail and q.dequeue() == 'C'
try:
    q.dequeue()
except IndexError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError('empty dequeue must raise')
print('PASS: refill and empty boundary')
challenges: Predict head and tail after enqueuing just one node.
Find the bug when dequeue never clears tail on the last item.
Repeat the operations using collections.deque.append and popleft.

simulation.prompt: What must be true after removing the last node?
choices: head and tail are both None
head is None but tail keeps the old node
simulation.explanation: Both pointers must represent the same empty state.

assessment.question: Which end does a FIFO linked queue remove from?
What happens to tail after the last node is removed?
assessment.explanation: The queue is empty and both pointers must say so.

assessment.question: What Python container usually replaces this custom queue in an app?
assessment.explanation: It already provides efficient append and popleft operations.
